Skip to article

Typography playground

Adjust the page as you read. Export your settings when it feels right.

Óia / Article specimen

The things we choose to keep

We collect things because they make us pause: a photograph, a sentence, a place we want to return to. A good reading page gives each of them enough room, and makes it easy to move from one thought to the next.

This specimen is deliberately ordinary. It has short paragraphs and longer ones, headings that wrap, images with captions, and a mix of strong emphasis, italic emphasis, and links that remain easy to find. The typography should feel comfortable through all of them.

A little space between ideas

A heading introduces the paragraph beneath it. It should read as part of the same thought, with enough distance from the previous section to make the transition clear.

Longer text makes spacing easier to judge. As the lines accumulate, the relationship between the letterforms, the line length, and the leading becomes more apparent. A narrow face may need a different measure from a broad one. A generous line height can help a dense font breathe, but too much makes a paragraph fall apart into separate lines.

There is a kind of attention that only becomes possible when nothing is asking you to hurry.

A sample quotation, written for this specimen

An inline quotation sits within a sentence: she described the place as a room with enough light to think, then went back to her notebook. It follows the body typography, with italics to distinguish the quoted words.

What a reading page has to hold

  • An idea that fits in one line.
  • A longer observation that wraps onto another line, so the hanging indent and line spacing have a chance to show themselves.
  • A few related details:
    • A small photograph.
    • A source worth returning to.
    • A fragment of a conversation.

Lists should feel connected without becoming a wall of text. The marker belongs to the line; wrapped text should sit beneath the words.

One thing after another

  1. Notice something worth keeping.
  2. Save the original, including its source and the details that give it meaning.
  3. Come back to it later, when a different question gives it a different use.
  4. Repeat with a nested sequence:
    1. Read slowly.
    2. Make a connection.

A few useful distinctions

Measure
The width of a line of text. A comfortable measure changes with the font, its size, and the language being read.
Leading
The distance between successive baselines. The controls use a multiplier of the chosen font size.
Rhythm
The relationship between lines, paragraphs, and sections as the eye moves down a page.

Comparing the pieces

A small table with text and numeric values
ElementPurposeExamples
ParagraphCarry the main thought3–8 lines
HeadingMark a new sectionH1 through H6
QuotationIntroduce another voice“A different perspective”
The table should remain easy to scan at every body size.
A technical aside

Inline code, such as font-size: 18px or reading.tags, should be distinct but stay at home inside a paragraph. The same applies to a keyboard shortcut like ⌘ + K and sample output like Saved locally.

article {
  font-family: var(--body-font);
  font-size: var(--body-size);
  line-height: var(--body-leading);
}

blockquote {
  font-family: var(--quote-font);
  /* A different voice, in the same page. */
}
The smallest heading still has a job

It introduces a modest piece of information without turning into another title. A small heading should remain readable and clearly connected to its paragraph.

Fine details and unfamiliar characters

A page can contain an API, a date such as 13 October 2026, a formula like H2O, and an exponent like 28. These small details should not knock the whole line out of shape.1

Sometimes text is highlighted for later, sometimes it is crossed out, and sometimes a correction is added in its place. There is room for a quiet aside as well as a thought that needs both weight and emphasis.

Á É Í Ó Ú · à è ì ò ù · å æ ø œ ß · Óia · Reykjavík · São Paulo
0123456789 · €19.50 · £240 · $1,280 · 2026–2027
“Double quotes” · ‘single quotes’ · apostrophes aren’t accents — and dashes matter…

An expandable note

The reading surface should still work when secondary content is revealed. This is a native HTML disclosure, with keyboard support and no custom interaction.

A few form elements

A small notebook

65%

72%

Returning to the page

The point of this exercise is to choose a reading rhythm you like. Try a different body face before changing its size. Then adjust the leading. Notice what happens to long paragraphs, short lists, and the quotation above.

For a useful comparison, keep the width steady while you change fonts. Once the type feels right, adjust the measure and the distance between paragraphs and sections.
